screens.body:
Injection is the #1 classic: attacker input gets treated as code. The famous example is SQL injection — typing `' OR '1'='1` into a login box tricks the query into matching every user.

The fix is boring and total: never build queries by gluing strings together. Use parameterized queries (placeholders), and the database treats input as data, always.

options: Treat input as data with parameterized queries
check.question: The fix for SQL injection:

screens.heading: Injection: when input becomes code
screens.keyPoint: Parameterize. Never glue strings into queries.

screens.body:
XSS — cross-site scripting — is injection's browser cousin: an attacker sneaks a script into YOUR page, and it runs in your VICTIMS' browsers. Steal sessions, deface pages, redirect to phishing.

Example: a comment box that renders raw HTML. Attacker posts <script>…, every visitor runs it. The fix: escape output — turn < into < so browsers display it instead of running it.

options: Attacker script running in victims' browsers via your page
check.question: XSS is…

screens.heading: XSS: your page, their script
screens.keyPoint: Escape output. Never render raw user HTML.

screens.body:
CSRF — cross-site request forgery — rides your login. You're logged into your bank; you visit evil.com; it silently submits a form to bank.com/transfer. Your browser attaches your cookies, and the bank thinks YOU asked.

Defenses: anti-CSRF tokens (a secret per form the attacker can't guess), SameSite cookies, and checking the Origin header. Frameworks often do this for you — don't turn it off.

options: Forged requests riding your logged-in session
check.question: CSRF is…

screens.heading: CSRF: the forged request
screens.keyPoint: Anti-CSRF tokens + SameSite cookies stop it.

screens.body:
Broken access control topped the OWASP Top 10 in 2021 — above injection. It means the app fails to check 'is this user allowed to do THIS?': changing the ID in a URL to view someone else's orders, or hitting an admin API directly.

The rule: check authorization on EVERY request, server-side. The frontend hiding a button is decoration, not security.

options: Server-side permission check on every request
check.question: What actually enforces access control?

screens.heading: #1: broken access control
screens.keyPoint: Check permission on every request, server-side.

screens.body:
Sensitive data exposure is leaking secrets where they don't belong: stack traces with database passwords shown to users, API keys in frontend code, personal data in logs, backups with no encryption.

Habit: treat error messages as public. Log the details server-side; show users a generic 'something went wrong.' And grep your repo for keys before every deploy.

options: Secrets in error messages, frontend code, or logs
check.question: Sensitive data exposure looks like…

screens.heading: Don't leak the secrets
screens.keyPoint: Errors are public. Log details, show generics.

screens.body:
Real attacks chain small flaws: an XSS steals an admin's session, broken access control lets the attacker reach the admin panel, and missing logging means nobody notices for months.

That's why defense in depth matters — one missed lock shouldn't open the vault. Each layer you add breaks a link in someone's chain.

options: Small flaws linked: XSS → session theft → admin access
check.question: How do real attacks usually work?

screens.heading: Attacks chain together
screens.keyPoint: Break one link and the whole chain fails.

screens.body:
Your defensive mindset in one screen: validate all input server-side, escape all output, parameterize queries, check auth on every request, keep secrets out of code, update dependencies.

You won't memorize every attack. But if these six habits are automatic, you'll block the vast majority of real-world breaches.

options: Only worry about it at launch
Validate, escape, parameterize, authorize, protect secrets, update
check.question: The six defensive habits:

screens.heading: Your defensive mindset
screens.keyPoint: Six habits block most real breaches.
